title: Eighty Years of Harvard Men
text:
In 1938, with funding from the businessman W. T. Grant, the Harvard physician Arlie Bock began following a group of 268 healthy Harvard undergraduates, the so-called Grant Study. The idea was to learn what helps people thrive, not just what makes them sick. The men were examined, interviewed and surveyed again and again for the rest of their lives. Their records were later combined with those of a second study, begun by Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck, of several hundred boys from poor neighborhoods of inner-city Boston.

The psychiatrist George Vaillant directed the study for over three decades, and Robert Waldinger later took it over and extended it to the participants' children. Researchers looked at careers, marriages, health, drinking, mood and much else as the men aged.

The finding they emphasized most was about relationships. The warmth of men's relationships, with parents in childhood, with spouses and with friends, predicted their health and happiness in old age better than social class, intelligence or wealth did. Men who were more satisfied in their relationships at age 50 were healthier at 80. Vaillant summed it up by saying that what mattered most in life was relationships with other people.
lesson: Over a lifetime, the quality of your relationships matters more for health and happiness than money or status. Invest in them steadily, not only when there is time.
people: Arlie Bock, George Vaillant, Robert Waldinger and colleagues
source: Vaillant, G. E. (2012). Triumphs of Experience: The Men of the Harvard Grant Study. Harvard University Press. See also Waldinger, R., and Schulz, M. (2023). The Good Life. Simon and Schuster.
caveat: The original samples were all men and almost all white, and the findings are correlational.
